node.label: Judith Butler
node.date_label: “Performative Acts and Gender Constitution” (1988) · Gender Trouble (1990) · Bodies That Matter (1993)
node.description: Investigates the historically repeated acts through which gender becomes intelligible and is enforced. The selected 1988 essay treats embodiment as the taking up of possibilities constrained by inherited conventions, rather than an act by an already independent will. Its final pages ask how feminist representation can acknowledge diverse experiences without fixing women as a uniform natural category. The same argument questions a compulsory binary and heterosexual framework while recognizing punitive sanctions on departures from it. These particular primary pages supplement the earlier publisher-level Gender Trouble record; they do not establish a complete reading of that book or every later revision of performativity.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Performative Acts and Gender Constitution” (1988); Gender Trouble (1990; new preface/reissue 1999 separate); Bodies That Matter (1993).

proposed_edges.relationship: Explains gendered embodiment through repeated, historically constrained acts and the sanctions that sustain apparently natural identities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 521–522 read from Stanford-hosted primary PDF text, supplemented by final pp. 530–531; no unrestricted personal choice or disembodied will.

proposed_edges.relationship: Questions the binary and implicitly heterosexual restrictions reproduced when a single category of women becomes theory’s unquestioned starting point.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 530–531 read. The argument preserves the political importance of representing women while contesting reification; not denial of lived experience or a fresh reading of every later queer-theory text.
